summary: Defines a Transport Subsystem for the SNMP architecture, a place for Transport Models comparable to the other subsystems in the SNMP architecture of RFC 3411. It makes it possible to run SNMP over transports beyond UDP, including secure ones.

eli5.summary: SNMP lets you check on network devices. This builds a slot so different delivery trucks, including locked ones, can carry the questions and answers.

questions: what is the snmp transport subsystem
what is a transport model in snmp
how does snmp use ssh or tls
subtitle: A pluggable slot in the SNMP architecture so management messages can ride over secure transports such as SSH and TLS.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 security (USM) needs its own user and key infrastructure, which operators found a deterrent to deploying it, and the RFC 3411 architecture had no place for transport models that bring their own security.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5590 adds a Transport Subsystem to the SNMP engine, defines sendMessage and receiveMessage interfaces, and adds a tmStateReference cache that carries transport security facts to security models.
tldr.outcome: SNMP can use existing security such as SSH or TLS in a modular way. It is an Internet Standard and updates RFC 3411, RFC 3412, RFC 3414 and RFC 3417.

today: RFC 5590 is an Internet Standard from June 2009 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 3411, RFC 3412, RFC 3414 and RFC 3417, and is used by RFC 5591 and RFC 5592.

sections.title: Why a Transport Subsystem
sections.content:
The RFC compares three ways to secure a building: sit on the porch yourself, hire and schedule your own guards, or hire a security company and leave the details to them. The User-based Security Model (USM) is the first approach. It provides all its own security, with a separate principal and key management infrastructure. Operators reported that deploying another such infrastructure was a deterrent to deploying SNMPv3, and they wanted to reuse user management that was not specific to SNMP.

Gluing external services such as RADIUS onto USM is the second approach and risks gaps between the differently subcontracted services. The RFC takes the third approach: let a lower-layer security protocol such as TLS, SASL or SSH do the message security. Operators also get one administrative security setup for SNMPv3, command line interfaces and other management interfaces.
sections.eli5: You can guard your house yourself, or hire a security company that already knows how. This RFC lets SNMP hire the security company (a tool like SSH or TLS) instead of doing everything on its own.

sections.title: Where the Subsystem Fits
sections.content:
RFC 3411 describes an SNMP engine built from a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem. It had no subsystem for transports, even though several transport mappings already existed in RFC 3417. RFC 5590 adds a Transport Subsystem that holds Transport Models such as UDP, TCP, SSH, TLS and others, which can be plugged in and advanced through the standards process independently.

Secure transports change the order of work. With existing models, security processing starts after the Message Processing Model decodes part of the message. A secure transport performs its security functions on the message before it is decoded, and some of those functions might then be repeated by the selected Security Model.

A secure Transport Model sets up an authenticated and possibly encrypted tunnel between two engines. Newer models MAY send many SNMP messages through the same tunnel to spread out the cost of setting up a security association.
sections.eli5: Think of the SNMP engine as a mail room with separate desks. This RFC adds a new desk by the front door where different kinds of mail trucks, including armored ones, can pull in.

sections.title: Requirements for a Transport Model
sections.content:
Transport security protocols SHOULD protect against four message threats from RFC 3411: modification of information, masquerade, message stream modification and disclosure. They should not make denial of service or traffic analysis significantly worse. A Transport Model SHOULD NOT require changes to the underlying protocol, and multiple Transport Models MUST be able to coexist.

A Transport Model MAY suggest values for securityName and securityLevel, but the Security Model decides whether to use them. Documents defining a new transport domain MUST define a prefix of one to four US-ASCII alphanumeric characters, which may be prepended to a securityName followed by a : character. That lets applications tell "alice" authenticated by SSH from "alice" authenticated by TLS.

On sessions, the model may keep a transport session open for many messages. There are no SNMP sessions in the architecture, and the subsystem never sees the PDU type. If a requested security level cannot be provided, the message should be discarded and the Dispatcher told. A Transport Model MAY upgrade the requested security level but MUST NOT downgrade it. It SHOULD discard the message if that would occur.

If a secure session closes between receiving a request and sending its response, the response SHOULD be discarded, even if a new session exists.
sections.eli5: The rules say the armored truck must be at least as safe as you asked for. It can be safer, never less safe. And if the truck that brought a question is gone, the answer is thrown away rather than sent in a different truck.

sections.title: The tmStateReference Cache
sections.content:
Security Models cannot see transport details through the old interfaces, so the RFC defines a cache. A tmStateReference parameter is passed between the Transport Subsystem and the Message Processing and Security Subsystems to say which cache to consult. The cache is only used inside an implementation, so its format is implementation-specific. A fully defined one MUST conceptually include seven fields: tmTransportDomain, tmTransportAddress, tmSecurityName, tmRequestedSecurityLevel, tmTransportSecurityLevel, tmSameSecurity and tmSessionID.

Three identities are involved: the transport principal (authenticated by the transport), the tmSecurityName (a readable name for it), and the securityName that applications and access control see. A non-transport-aware Security Model ignores tmSecurityName completely.

Two level fields keep two ideas apart. tmTransportSecurityLevel says what the session offers, and tmRequestedSecurityLevel says what the Security Model needs. The tmSameSecurity flag and tmSessionID support the rule about responses: if the flag is true when sending, the session ID MUST match the current session or the message MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: The cache is a sticky note attached to each delivery. It says who the sender really is and how well locked the truck was, so the next desk can read it.

sections.title: New and Changed Interfaces
sections.content:
RFC 3411 had no interface for the arrows labelled "Send SNMP message to Network" and "Receive SNMP message from Network". RFC 5590 defines two Abstract Service Interfaces (ASIs) for them. sendMessage passes a message from the Dispatcher to the Transport Model, with the destination domain and address, the message, its length and a tmStateReference. receiveMessage passes a received message the other way. The Transport Model does not know the security model of an incoming message, since the Message Processing Model determines it. Both ASIs are used for all SNMP messages regardless of PDU type.

The document also adds a tmStateReference parameter to existing RFC 3411 ASIs. It is an OUT parameter on prepareOutgoingMessage, prepareResponseMessage, generateRequestMsg and generateResponseMsg, and an IN parameter on prepareDataElements and processIncomingMsg. The latter two also gain transport domain and address parameters on the sending side. How or whether a model uses the cache is specific to that model.
sections.eli5: Two new doorways are added: one for mail going out and one for mail coming in. The sticky note is also added to the forms the desks already pass around.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Each proposed Transport Model should discuss its own security considerations, including whether perfect forward secrecy is appropriate and how it behaves under denial of service. Because the cache holds security parameters, implementers SHOULD protect it from unauthorized disclosure and modification. An engine with several open transports must make sure it sends only with credentials it may legally use for that user.

The RFC says that using a non-transport-aware Security Model (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or USM) with a secure Transport Model is NOT RECOMMENDED. Those models see only security parameters in the SNMP message, so access control is based on, for example, an unauthenticated community name or an unauthenticated USM user with noAuthNoPriv, and not on the authenticated transport identity.

Secure transports may fail when services they depend on (such as NTP, AAA or certificate authorities) are unreachable. USM does not depend on external network services, so the RFC RECOMMENDS provisioning authPriv USM as a fallback.
sections.eli5: Do not pair a strong lock with a guard who only checks a name written on the box. And keep a spare key system that works even when the phones are down.

sections.title: The Transport Domains Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a registry called "SNMP Transport Domains" in the SNMP Number Spaces. Entries are strings of one to four US-ASCII alphanumeric characters that serve as prefixes. Each transport domain MUST have an OID under snmpDomains, and new values are assigned by "Specification Required".

The initial entries are udp, clns, cons, ddp, ipx and prxy, each tied to a domain defined in RFC 3417 (prxy maps to rfc1157Domain).
sections.eli5: Each kind of delivery truck gets a short nickname in an official list, so nobody mixes up two trucks with the same name.

items.title: tmTransportDomain
items.text: The transport protocol, and so the Transport Model, used for the message.

items.title: tmTransportAddress
items.text: The source of the incoming message.

items.title: tmSecurityName
items.text: A readable name for the transport-authenticated identity.

items.title: tmRequestedSecurityLevel
items.text: What the Security Model requires from the transport.

items.title: tmTransportSecurityLevel
items.text: What the transport session actually offers.

items.title: tmSameSecurity
items.text: If true, the response must use the same session as the request.

items.title: tmSessionID
items.text: Lets the Transport Model check whether the session changed.
